heroHeadline: One Year Since Ceasefire: Competing Victory Narratives, Zero Diplomatic Contact — Both Sides Claim 'Marka-e-Haq' and 'Operation Sindoor' Wins as Bilateral Freeze Holds Total
heroSubtitle: May 10, 2026 marks one year since the US-brokered ceasefire ended the India-Pakistan Operation Sindoor / Marka-e-Haq exchange. Both capitals held competing commemorations: India's IAF posted strike footage and PM Modi reaffirmed resolve against terrorism; Pakistan's Air Force held a ceremony at Nur Khan Auditorium while the week-long national Marka-e-Haq information campaign culminated. Al Jazeera captured the dynamic with 'Two wins, two losses: What India and Pakistan have learned a year after war.' The bilateral freeze remains total one year on: mutual airspace closure extended to May 24, Indus Waters Treaty suspended (Pakistan escalated to UNSC on April 24), all direct trade halted, no ambassadors exchanged. Pakistan's post-conflict rearmament has accelerated: Army Rocket Force Command (ARFC) formally operationalized managing Fatah-3 and Shaheen systems; Taimoor air-launched cruise missile (600 km) successfully tested in January 2026 and fired from a naval platform in April 2026; 40 J-35A stealth fighters on order from China. No active US-mediated India-Pakistan diplomatic process exists; Washington's bandwidth has shifted toward Iran. The Washington Post assessed the ceasefire is holding 'so far' — but with unresolved root causes (cross-border terrorism, Kashmir, Indus Waters, competing narratives) making conflict re-ignition a significant risk.
footerNote: Data sourced from Indian MEA/MOD, Pakistan ISPR/MFA, UN Security Council, SIPRI, Crisis Group, HRW, Stimson Center
